Minnesota, like all states, uses an exclusion adjusted cohort graduation indicator (EACGI) model to calculate graduation rates. This model assigns each student to a cohort when they first enroll in public high school in Minnesota, which is typically in ninth grade, but can be in tenth, eleventh, or twelfth grade for students who move to Minnesota from other states or countries or who transfer from private schools to public schools. When a student transfers from one Minnesota public high school to another, they enter their new school's graduation cohort and leave their previous school's cohort. When a student leaves the state or country, transfers to a private school, or dies, they are removed from their most recent cohort.

At the end of a cohort's timeline -- for example, at the end of four years for a four-year cohort or the end of seven years for a seven-year cohort -- students who are still in the cohort are counted as graduating, continuing, dropping out, or unknown in their last school's graduation rate, with two exceptions.

Exception 1: Students who drop out of a school after less than half a school year are included in the cohort of the school where they spent the most time during their high school years. This only applies to students who drop out (not to students who graduate, continue, or are unknown), and only after less than half a school year.

Exception 2: Students who, at the end of their last school year in a cohort - for example, the fourth school year in their four-year cohort - have not graduated, but who go on to graduate over the summer, are included as graduates at whichever school they completed their last graduation requirement. This only applies to students who graduate over the summer; other summer enrollments do not have an impact on graduation rates.

Student Identification: The Minnesota Department of Education (MDE) is now reporting students using eight state-defined racial and ethnic groups, including the use of the state definition of American Indian and the new Other Indigenous group. The tabs labeled "State," "County," "District," and "School" report students using these groups. In these tabs, students count as American Indian if they meet the state definition regardless of any other racial or ethnic groups with which they may have identified. The state of Minnesota’s definition of American Indian includes any of the original people within what is now the borders of the United States (excluding Hawaii) or Canada who maintain cultural identification through tribal affiliation or community recognition.

This is different from the federal definition of American Indian or Alaska Native which includes students whose only racial or ethnic identification is with the original peoples of North, Central, or South America. Within the eight state racial or ethnic groups, the new Other Indigenous group includes students who meet the federal definition of American Indian or Alaska Native but not the state definition of American Indian, which means they identify only with indigenous peoples from Central and South America.
